title: Practice: keep every library request
vision: Apply ordering and preservation to a library queue where equal priorities still represent different requests.
explanation: Laws and generation strategies are authored in LawSpec. Only the implementation changes language.
news: Equal priority values can represent separate requests that must both survive.
contributions: A library queue sorter with ordering and occurrence preservation. Duplicate requests survive; replacing requests with zeros fails even when the output length is right.

star.salient: Equal priority values can represent separate requests that must both survive.
star.surprise: A queue can have the right length and be ordered while every priority has been replaced.
star.story: The library needs requests ordered by priority. Empty output, deduplication and invented zero priorities all lose the meaning of the queue; a correct sort preserves every request’s rank.

stages.title: What does one number in the queue mean?
story: A library serves requests by priority. For this exercise, each integer represents one request’s priority rank; a lower rank comes first. Two requests can have the same rank. They are still two requests.
The task is to reorder these ranks without dropping or inventing a request. By the end, you will have applied both parts of the sorting contract to that practical meaning.

The current implementation returns an empty queue, and Laws asks only whether its output is ordered. Predict whether that check rejects it, then run checks with All checks. An empty result has no out-of-order pair, but nobody remains in the queue.
stages.action: Run the ordering-only suite. Explain what each of the two 1s represents and why [] fails the library’s task.
stages.reason: Priority is the sorting key, not a request identity. Equal keys do not authorize deleting a request.

stages.title: Two requests with one priority must both stay
story: Laws now requires sameItems as well as ordered. The concrete “requests with equal priority both stay” check contains two requests with rank 1 and one with rank 3.

Solution removes repeated values before sorting. That treats the two rank-1 requests as if they were the same request. Use Run checks with All checks: the result is ordered, but one request has disappeared.
This is preservation: every input occurrence has a matching output occurrence. It is different from merely checking whether each distinct value appears somewhere.

stages.reason: Same priority, separate requests. Sorting a queue must preserve the count at each rank.

stages.title: Invented priorities are not preservation
story: This implementation returns a zero for every input item. It keeps the number of positions, and those zeros are ordered.
The requests’ priority ranks have been replaced. Run the unchanged suite and inspect which counts disagree. The sameItems requirement catches this without adding a special rule against zero.

stages.title: Deliver the ordered queue
story: The starter returns the ranks unchanged. It retains every request but leaves an out-of-order queue out of order. Run it to see the remaining failure.
Implement a sort that satisfies both requirements, then rerun checks with All checks. Keep the two rank-1 requests in the named example.

As your own challenge, write a case with three requests sharing one rank and another request at a different rank. Predict the result and check both counts and order. You will have tests that distinguish equal priority from duplicate identity.

implementationSyntax.fsharp: In F#, List.sort orders ranks; List.distinct removes equal values, which loses separate requests at the same rank.
implementationSyntax.typescript: In TypeScript, number[] holds the ranks. A numeric comparator orders them; new Set removes equal values, losing requests at the same rank.
implementationSyntax.javascript: In JavaScript, the array holds the ranks. A numeric comparator orders them; new Set removes equal values, losing requests at the same rank.
